title: LATERAL joins, top-N per group and keyset pagination
goal: By the end, you can write a small query that runs once for each row of a table (LATERAL), pick the top few rows of every group three ways and say what each does with ties, and page through a million rows so that page 5,001 costs the same as page 1.
opening:
Picture scrolling back through a long list on your phone: your card payments, newest first, 20 at a time. The first pages appear at once. Far back in the list, each new page takes a little longer. And once, a coffee you saw a moment ago turns up again at the top of the next page.

A list like that comes from a payments app, a program that records every card payment people make at shops. It's tempting to think of page 5,001 as a place, like page 300 of a book, that the database can open at once. It can't, and the reason is how a database finds rows.

In Window frames and gaps-and-islands, every row read the rows around it, in one pass over the table. Many screens want less: three rows per shop, or the next 20 rows. In this lesson, we'll get the top three of every group three ways, and make page 5,001 cost no more than page 1. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The company's support staff have a screen that lists 1,000,000 payments, newest first, 20 per page. The database keeps an index for that order: a separate sorted list of every payment's time and id, each with a pointer to its row. Page 5,001 asks to skip the first 100,000 payments (`LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000`). About how many index entries does PostgreSQL read?
options: 20: the index lets it jump straight to entry 100,001
About 100,020
About 40: one trip down the index, then 20 entries
warmup.why: An index is sorted, but it doesn't store positions, so there's no entry 100,001 to jump to. OFFSET makes PostgreSQL read the first 100,000 entries in order, throw them away, and return the next 20. On the course's large data set, that's 100,020 rows and 2,865 buffers, the 8 KB pieces of storage the database reads. The first option is the book picture from the opening, and it's the trap. The last option describes a keyset cursor, which the last section builds: it goes straight to the last row of the previous page instead of counting.

sections.h: Each shop's three biggest sales: a subquery that runs once per row
sections.body:
Let's start with a screen the company wants: every shop with its three biggest sales. The app keeps its data in PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run. A database keeps data in tables, like sheets in a spreadsheet: each row is one record, and each column holds one piece of it. You ask it questions in SQL, the language most databases understand.

Two tables matter here. `merchants` has one row per shop (the app calls shops merchants), with its id and name: Northwind Grocers, Blue Fern Cafe, Metro Transit and five more. `payments` has one row per card payment, with the shop it paid (`merchant_id`), the amount in cents, the time, and a status that is `succeeded` when the money moved.

The question is per shop: for every row of `merchants`, a small query that depends on that shop. The FROM part of a query names what it reads. The first attempt puts the small query in FROM as a subquery, a query inside a query (Subqueries and common table expressions). `merchants m` gives the shops table the short name `m`, and the subquery refers to it:

```sql
SELECT m.merchant_id, t.payment_id, t.amount_minor
FROM merchants m
CROSS JOIN (SELECT payment_id, amount_minor
            FROM payments p
            WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND p.status = 'succeeded'
            ORDER BY amount_minor DESC, payment_id
            LIMIT 3) AS t;
```

Inside the subquery, `ORDER BY amount_minor DESC, payment_id` sorts the payments biggest first (DESC means descending), with the payment's id to break ties, and `LIMIT 3` keeps the first three. `CROSS JOIN` pairs every row on its left with every row on its right. PostgreSQL rejects the query, and its hint names the fix:

```postgresql
ERROR:  invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "m"
DETAIL:  There is an entry for table "m", but it cannot be referenced from this part of the query.
HINT:  To reference that table, you must mark this subquery with LATERAL.
```

The tables and subqueries in FROM are independent. Each one is worked out on its own, and only then are they joined. So the subquery may not mention `m`, the shop beside it, and without that condition it would return the three biggest payments of all. A subquery in the SELECT list, the values a query returns for each row, may mention `m`, because it runs again for each row. But it must return one value, and three payments fail with `more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression`.

The keyword `LATERAL` in front of a subquery in FROM lets it use the tables to its left. PostgreSQL then runs it once for each of their rows, with that row's values plugged in, and joins each row to whatever rows its run returned. Write `CROSS JOIN LATERAL (...)` in the query above and it works. In Kotlin it's a `flatMap`: for each shop, build a small list, then join all the lists into one.

```kotlin
merchants.flatMap { m ->
    payments.filter { it.merchantId == m.id && it.status == "succeeded" }
        .sortedWith(compareByDescending<Payment> { it.amountMinor }.thenBy { it.paymentId })
        .take(3)
        .map { m to it }                     // join each returned row to its merchant
}
```

That's the picture for this lesson: **for each outer row, run the inner query with that row's values, and join the rows it returns.** Picture a filing cabinet full of receipts, with a list of shop names taped to the front. For each name, you search the cabinet for that shop's receipts and pull out the three biggest. The list is `merchants`, each search is one run of the subquery, and the three receipts are the rows it returns. The stepper runs it shop by shop.

The result has 18 rows for 6 shops. Paper Lantern Books (6) and Sunrise Grocers (8) are missing: their runs returned nothing, and CROSS JOIN drops a row that has no partner. `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) AS t ON true` keeps them, with NULL, the database's word for no value, in the payment columns. ON gives the condition for pairing rows, and LEFT JOIN must have one, so `ON true` fills the slot; the subquery has already done the matching.

A function in FROM can always use earlier columns, keyword or not. Each payment's `metadata` column holds a small document from the fraud check, a program that scores each payment and lists the warning rules that fired. `p.metadata -> 'risk' -> 'rules'` picks that list out of the document, and `CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements_text(...) AS r (rule)` turns it into one row per rule. The next lesson opens those documents up.

One small query per shop is one way to get a top three. Next, we'll meet two more, and see what each one does when two payments tie.

sections.h: The top three of every group, three ways, and what each does with ties
sections.body:
The shop screen is one case of a question you'll meet often: the top N rows of each group, for a small N. The newest payment per card, the three biggest shops per country, the latest login per customer. PostgreSQL gives you three ways to write it, and they differ in what they do with ties, in which groups appear, and in cost.

The window way, from Window functions: ranking, LAG and running totals, numbers the rows inside each group and keeps the first N one level up. A window function computes a value for each row from other rows and keeps every row. `row_number()` is one that numbers rows 1, 2, 3 in the order its `OVER (...)` part gives, and `PARTITION BY merchant_id` starts again at 1 for each shop:

```sql
SELECT merchant_id, payment_id, amount_minor
FROM (SELECT merchant_id, payment_id, amount_minor,
             row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY merchant_id
                                ORDER BY amount_minor DESC, payment_id) AS place
      FROM payments
      WHERE status = 'succeeded') AS ranked
WHERE place <= 3;
```

The numbering sits in an inner query because WHERE, which keeps the rows that pass a test, runs before window functions. The outer query is the first place that can see `place`.

The LATERAL way, from the first section, runs one small query per shop, with LIMIT 3 to keep its first three rows.

The DISTINCT ON way works for N = 1. `SELECT DISTINCT ON (merchant_id) ...` keeps the first row of each set of rows with the same merchant_id, and "first" means first in the query's ORDER BY. So the ORDER BY must start with the DISTINCT ON columns, then go on with whatever picks the winner: `ORDER BY merchant_id, amount_minor DESC, payment_id`. Start it with anything else and PostgreSQL refuses: `SELECT DISTINCT ON expressions must match initial ORDER BY expressions`. DISTINCT ON belongs to PostgreSQL alone, not to standard SQL (the part every database shares), and it's the shortest way to write "the latest row per key".

The three agree only if they agree on ties. Metro Transit (shop 3) sells bus and train rides, and it has one 5.50 ride and three 2.75 rides. So its top three cut through a tie: 550, then two of the three 275s. With `payment_id` as the tiebreaker, row_number and LIMIT both keep payments 4 and 9 and drop 26. Without it, which 275 stays is up to the database, and it can change from run to run.

If tied rows should all stay, filter on `rank() <= 3` instead. rank gives tied rows the same place, so Metro Transit gets four rows. Or write `FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS WITH TIES` inside the LATERAL subquery, which keeps going while rows tie with the third. **Decide what a tie means before you write a top three.** None of the three ways warns you when you forget; each one quietly keeps whichever rows come first.

They also differ in which groups appear. The window and DISTINCT ON ways start from payments, so a shop without payments has no rows to number and never appears. The LATERAL way starts from the shops, so LEFT JOIN LATERAL can keep every one. When the screen must list every shop, start from the shops table.

On 37 payments, all three answer in a blink. Next, we'll run them on a million and see which one stays fast.

sections.h: Which way is fast: one big sort, or a few rows per shop from an index
sections.body:
On 37 payments, every way finishes in a few milliseconds at most. The course also has a large data set, a generated copy of the same tables with a million payments at 2,500 shops. There the three ways behave very differently, and the reason is how many rows each one has to read.

The window way reads every succeeded payment, 930,826 rows, and sorts them all by shop and amount before row_number can count. It does that whether you want the top 3 or the top 300, and it takes about 1 to 3 seconds on a laptop.

The LATERAL way runs its small query 2,500 times. With no help, each run reads the whole payments table to find one shop's rows, then sorts them. Twenty shops took about 4 to 9 seconds, so all 2,500 would take many minutes, long enough for a coffee at Blue Fern Cafe. In the cabinet picture, that's searching every drawer again for each name on the list. Subqueries and common table expressions met the same problem: an inner query that runs once per outer row, and reads a big table each time.

An index changes that. For now, an **index** is a separate structure that keeps chosen columns in sorted order, each entry with a pointer to its row. In the cabinet, it's a folder per shop with its receipts filed biggest first. With an index on `(merchant_id, amount_minor DESC, payment_id)`, each shop's payments sit together, in exactly the order the subquery wants. "The three biggest payments of shop 1000" becomes: find shop 1000's first entry, read three entries, follow three pointers. The Storage engines and query execution track shows how an index is built.

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs a query and prints its plan: the steps PostgreSQL chose, how many rows each produced and how often it ran. Here the plan is a Nested Loop over the 2,500 shops, which runs the inner step once per shop, with an Index Scan, a read through the index, inside: `rows=3.00 loops=2500`. The whole query took between 0.04 and 0.7 seconds, depending on whether the index was already in memory.

So, a rule of thumb. When the groups are big, you want a few rows from each, and an index matches the inner ORDER BY, use LATERAL with LIMIT. When there's no such index, or you need most of each group anyway, the window's one big sort is cheaper. Look at the plan before you decide.

One more measurement from the same session is worth knowing. With the index in place, PostgreSQL chose to feed the window way from the index too, to skip the sort, and it got slower: 5 to 10 seconds. Reading a whole table through an index visits its rows in index order, one jump at a time, all over the table. A plain read goes through the table from start to end, and the sort then runs in memory and in temporary files. An index helps when it lets you read less. When you have to read everything, reading the table in its own order and sorting is often faster.

Indexes find rows by their values. Next, we'll ask one for a row by its position, page 5,001, and watch what it does.

sections.h: Page 5,001 the slow way: OFFSET reads every row it skips
sections.body:
Back to the list from the opening. The company's support staff have a screen that lists payments newest first, 20 per page, with page numbers at the bottom. The obvious query for a page uses LIMIT and OFFSET:

```sql
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;          -- page 5,001
```

`ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC` sorts newest first (DESC means descending), and payment_id breaks ties. LIMIT 20 keeps 20 rows. OFFSET 100000 means "skip the first 100,000 rows of the result". To skip a row, PostgreSQL has to produce it first. Its documentation says so: the rows skipped by OFFSET still have to be computed inside the server.

Picture the payments as receipts filed in one long drawer, by time. To hand someone the 100,001st receipt, you count from the front, because no receipt has its position written on it. An index is the same. It stores keys and pointers, not row numbers, so there's no way to jump to entry 100,001. Here the cabinet picture breaks. A person could at least open the drawer near the middle by feel. An index can't even guess.

With an index on `(created_at, payment_id)`, page 1 reads the newest 20 entries and stops. That's 5 buffers and a fraction of a millisecond; a buffer is one 8 KB page, the unit PostgreSQL reads and keeps in memory. Page 5,001 walks the index from the newest entry through 100,020 entries, fetches each row, throws away 100,000 and returns 20: 2,865 buffers and about 50 ms. Page 45,001 read 900,020 rows and took 1.2 seconds. The cost grows with the page number. Without the index it's worse: every page sorts the whole table.

OFFSET is also wrong when rows arrive while someone pages, and in a payments app rows always arrive. Page 1 shows payments 37 to 33. A new payment comes in. Page 2, OFFSET 5, now starts one row earlier than it would have, so it shows payment 33 a second time: the coffee from the opening. A deleted row does the opposite, and the next page skips a row nobody saw. A nightly export that copies the table page by page with OFFSET can copy a payment twice or miss one, and no error says so. It's an easy trap, because page numbers seem to ask for OFFSET, and with a few hundred test rows every page is fast and nothing moves.

The figure shows both queries on the same index. The OFFSET query reads its way to the page. The second query, from the next section, jumps there.

**Counting your way to a page gets slower and shifts. Find the page by a key.**

The screen already knows where the last page ended: the last row it showed. Next, we'll ask for the rows after that row.

sections.h: Page 5,001 the fast way: start after the last row you showed
sections.body:
Give the screen a cursor: the sort key of the last row on the page, here its created_at and payment_id. (The sort key is the set of columns the list is sorted by.) For the next page, ask for the rows that come after that key in the sort order:

```sql
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE (created_at, payment_id) < (:last_created_at, :last_payment_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

`:last_created_at` and `:last_payment_id` stand for the cursor's two values. `(a, b) < (x, y)` is a **row comparison**. PostgreSQL compares the pairs left to right and stops at the first pair that differs. That's how you'd compare two dates: by year first, and by day only if the years match. Kotlin's `compareBy({ it.createdAt }, { it.paymentId })` does the same. A payment comes before the cursor if its created_at is earlier, or if the created_at is equal and its payment_id is smaller. Because the list is newest first, "before" in value means "after" on the screen.

This is **keyset pagination**, also called the seek method. With the index on `(created_at, payment_id)`, PostgreSQL goes down the index once, to the cursor's place, and reads the next 20 entries. That's the same work on page 2 and on page 5,001. EXPLAIN shows the row comparison as an `Index Cond`, a condition the index itself answers, and 5 buffers, about a millisecond or less, where OFFSET needed 2,865. New payments shift nothing: they sort before the cursor and show up on page 1. In the cabinet, the cursor is a tab clipped behind the last receipt you handed over. Next time, you open the drawer at the tab.

Three details decide whether it's correct. The ORDER BY must be unique, which is why payment_id is in it: two payments in the same instant are rare in a test and normal in a batch. The WHERE must use the whole row comparison. `WHERE created_at < :last_created_at` alone skips every remaining payment that shares the cursor's created_at, and nothing tells you. And the ORDER BY, the row comparison and the index must agree in column order and direction. Mixed directions, such as created_at DESC with payment_id ASC, can't be written as one row comparison.

The spelled-out form `created_at < :t OR (created_at = :t AND payment_id < :id)` returns the same rows, but PostgreSQL 18 didn't go straight to the cursor with it. EXPLAIN showed it as a Filter, a check on each row read, which read and threw away 100,000 index entries, as many as OFFSET. So write the row comparison.

You give up page numbers. A cursor moves forward one page at a time, and backward if you flip the comparison and the sort, but it can't jump to page 4,000. For an endless scroll, a nightly export, or an API (the way other programs ask yours for data) that hands back a `next` token for the next page, that costs nothing. Hand the cursor out as an opaque token: the two values packed into one string, for example in base64, a way to write any bytes as plain text. Then other programs can't build cursors of their own and come to depend on the format.

That leaves one limit on everything in this lesson. LATERAL with LIMIT, DISTINCT ON and keyset pages are fast only when an index matches the query's WHERE and ORDER BY, column for column. Indexes and reading EXPLAIN, in the Storage engines and query execution track, shows why that order matters.

a.src:
-- Oracle cannot apply < to a row value (ORA-01796),
-- so the cursor is spelled out: a range the index can
-- use, minus the rows already shown
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE created_at <= :last_created_at
  AND NOT (created_at = :last_created_at
           AND payment_id >= :last_payment_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.src:
-- one row comparison: the whole cursor is the
-- Index Cond of a single index scan
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE (created_at, payment_id)
      < (:last_created_at, :last_payment_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
LIMIT 20;           -- FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY also works

compare.note: Both return the same page. Oracle is another database program, sold by the company of the same name and run by many banks and large firms. Use The Index, Luke, a well-known guide to SQL indexes, reports that Oracle accepts row values, the `(a, b)` pairs, but can't use `<` on them, and fails with ORA-01796. Its workaround is on the left. `created_at <= :t` is a plain range on the index's first column, so the index can go straight to the cursor's time, and the NOT removes the few rows at that time that were already shown. PostgreSQL can use a row comparison directly as an index condition, so one condition says it all. `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` is the standard spelling of LIMIT and works in both; old Oracle code pages with nested queries on ROWNUM, Oracle's row counter, instead. For the per-row subqueries of this lesson, Oracle 12c added LATERAL and two joins called CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY. OUTER APPLY is PostgreSQL's LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true.

worked.title: From many queries to one: the latest payment for every shop

steps.say: A program that draws the shop screen could ask the database one question at a time. It loads the shops, then asks for each shop's latest succeeded payment, one query per shop. The code below does that from Kotlin through JDBC, Java's standard way for a program to send SQL to a database and read the answer. Each query is a round trip: the question travels to the database and the answer travels back. That's 1 + N round trips for N shops, the N+1 problem: 9 on the test data and 2,501 on the large data set, each one waiting on the network.

The loop body is the LATERAL subquery. The `?` becomes `m.merchant_id`, the loop becomes the outer table, and LEFT JOIN with `ON true` keeps the shops whose query found nothing, as the Kotlin code kept them with a null.
steps.code:
-- 2. the loop body, moved into the statement
SELECT m.merchant_id, m.name, last.payment_id, last.amount_minor, last.created_at
FROM merchants m
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount_minor, p.created_at
    FROM payments p
    WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND p.status = 'succeeded'
    ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.payment_id DESC
    LIMIT 1
) AS last ON true

steps.say: The screen also wants each shop's number of succeeded payments in June, the 30 days before 1 July. A second LATERAL can count them. An aggregate such as count with no GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, even over no rows (the count is then 0), so CROSS JOIN is safe here and drops no shop.
steps.code:
-- 3. a second per-merchant subquery: one aggregate row each
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT count(*) AS payments_30d
    FROM payments p
    WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND p.status = 'succeeded'
      AND p.created_at >= timestamptz '2026-07-01' - interval '30 days'
      AND p.created_at <  timestamptz '2026-07-01'
) AS recent
ORDER BY m.merchant_id;   -- and add recent.payments_30d to the SELECT list

steps.say: One statement, one round trip, all eight shops. On the large data set, the same statement does 2,500 index lookups inside the database instead of 2,501 trips over the network, given an index on `(merchant_id, created_at, payment_id)` for the inner ORDER BY.

drill.title: A keyset page for one card, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the query for the next page of card 8's payments, newest first, 20 per page, after a page that ended with payment 18 (made at 2026-03-12 16:42:10 UTC). Then write the index that lets PostgreSQL go straight to the cursor.

answer.src:
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE card_id = 8                                                      -- the group being paged
  AND (created_at, payment_id) < (timestamptz '2026-03-12 16:42:10+00', 18)   -- after the cursor
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC                              -- unique, same columns and direction
LIMIT 20;
-- 17 | 2026-03-12 16:40:00+00 | 18999
--  6 | 2026-01-22 12:05:00+00 |  2150

-- equality column first, then the sort key in the same order; read backward for DESC
CREATE INDEX payments_card_created_idx ON payments (card_id, created_at, payment_id);

recap: LATERAL lets a subquery in FROM use the tables to its left. PostgreSQL runs it once for each of their rows and joins each row to what its run returned.
CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops a row whose run returned nothing. LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) ON true keeps it, with NULLs.
Top N per group: row_number in an inner query, LATERAL with LIMIT, or DISTINCT ON for N = 1. Decide what ties mean, and say it with a tiebreaker, rank or WITH TIES.
LATERAL with LIMIT is fast when an index matches its ORDER BY: a few index entries per group. Without one, the window's single sort is cheaper.

OFFSET reads and throws away every row it skips, and its pages shift when rows arrive. Keyset pagination starts after the last row shown, with a row comparison on a unique sort key and an index in the same order.
The limit: all of this is fast only when an index matches the query's WHERE and ORDER BY, and a keyset cursor can't jump to page 4,000.
closing:
We started with a list that slowed down far back and showed a coffee twice. Both came from OFFSET, which counts its way to a page through every row before it. A cursor, the last row shown, goes straight to the next page, and a small query run once per row gave every shop its top three.

Next time a website shows you a long list, go to the next page and look at the web address. A `page=` number often means OFFSET underneath, and a long jumble of letters is often a keyset cursor.

Next, we'll stop only reading rows and start writing them, and find out how to store a payment message that arrives twice exactly once.

quiz.q: The shop screen must list every shop with its single biggest payment, including shops with no payments. Which FROM clause does that?
options: `merchants m CROSS JOIN LATERAL (... WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id ORDER BY amount_minor DESC LIMIT 1) t`
`merchants m LEFT JOIN LATERAL (... WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id ORDER BY amount_minor DESC LIMIT 1) t ON true`
`(SELECT DISTINCT ON (merchant_id) ... FROM payments ORDER BY merchant_id, amount_minor DESC) t`
`merchants m JOIN (SELECT ... FROM payments ORDER BY amount_minor DESC LIMIT 1) t ON t.merchant_id = m.merchant_id`
quiz.why: LEFT JOIN LATERAL runs the subquery per shop and keeps a shop whose run returned nothing. CROSS JOIN LATERAL, the tempting first option, drops it. DISTINCT ON starts from payments, so shops without payments never appear. The last one takes the single biggest payment of all and joins one shop to it.

quiz.q: Which payment per card does `SELECT DISTINCT ON (card_id) card_id, payment_id FROM payments ORDER BY card_id, created_at` return?
options: The card's latest payment
An arbitrary payment, because DISTINCT ON ignores ORDER BY
The card's earliest payment
None: it fails without DESC
quiz.why: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each card in the ORDER BY, and `created_at` sorted from oldest to newest puts the earliest first. DISTINCT ON never ignores the ORDER BY; it depends on it. For the latest, write `ORDER BY card_id, created_at DESC, payment_id DESC`. The payment_id fixes the winner when two payments share a time.

quiz.q: A page ended with the payment (created_at 10:00:00, id 500). The next page uses `WHERE created_at < '10:00:00' ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC LIMIT 20`. Payments 498 and 499 were also made at 10:00:00. What happens to them?
options: They appear first on the next page
They appear on the next page in random order
The query fails because created_at is not unique
They are never shown: the condition excludes every row at 10:00:00
quiz.why: Comparing created_at alone treats the whole second as already shown, so rows that tie with the cursor but sort after it are skipped for good, with no error. The query doesn't fail, because nothing in it asks for a unique time. `(created_at, payment_id) < ('10:00:00', 500)` includes them, because for equal times it compares the ids.

quiz.q: With an index on (created_at, payment_id), why does `ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` still read 100,020 index entries?
options: The index keeps entries sorted but stores no positions, so PostgreSQL must count its way to entry 100,001
OFFSET disables the use of indexes
PostgreSQL locks the skipped rows first
PostgreSQL can't read an index backward
quiz.why: An index can find a key quickly, but it can't find a position. OFFSET is a position, so the scan starts at the newest entry and counts. The plan in the Try it used the index, read backward, and still read 100,020 rows, so OFFSET doesn't switch indexes off. A keyset condition gives the scan a key to go to instead.

quiz.q: Subqueries and common table expressions showed a correlated subquery, one that reads values from the outer row, as a SubPlan: a step that runs once per outer row. How does a LATERAL subquery relate to it?
options: It doesn't read the outer row, so it runs once, like an InitPlan (a subquery PostgreSQL runs only once)
It is a correlated subquery placed in FROM: it runs per row of the tables to its left and may return many rows and columns
PostgreSQL always turns it into a hash join
It can return only one row, like a subquery in the SELECT list
quiz.why: Both are correlated: they read values from an outer row. A subquery in the SELECT list must return one value; a LATERAL subquery returns a small table, joined to the row it ran for. Like the SubPlan, it's cheap when each run uses an index and slow when each run reads a big table. There's no fixed join type: PostgreSQL picks a plan for each query.

flashcards.back: A subquery in FROM may use the tables to its left. PostgreSQL runs it once for each of their rows.

flashcards.front: CROSS JOIN LATERAL or LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true?
flashcards.back: CROSS drops outer rows whose run returned nothing. LEFT keeps them with NULLs; the ON true is only there because LEFT JOIN needs an ON.

flashcards.front: What must the ORDER BY of a DISTINCT ON query start with?
flashcards.back: The DISTINCT ON columns. The columns after them decide which row of each group is kept.

flashcards.front: Three ways to get the top N rows per group?
flashcards.back: row_number() in an inner query with `WHERE place <= N`; LATERAL with ORDER BY and LIMIT N; DISTINCT ON for N = 1.

flashcards.front: Why is OFFSET slow on deep pages?
flashcards.back: Skipped rows are still read and thrown away: page 5,001 of 20 rows reads 100,020. An index stores keys, not positions.

flashcards.front: What is the keyset condition for the next page, newest first?
flashcards.back: `WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n`, with an index on (created_at, id).

flashcards.front: Why must a keyset cursor include a unique column?
flashcards.back: Without it, rows that tie with the cursor's value are skipped or shown twice. The unique column makes every position exact.

terms.plain: A keyword that lets a subquery in FROM use the tables before it; it runs once per row of them.
The first N rows of each group in some order, such as each shop's three biggest payments.
PostgreSQL's way to keep the first row, by ORDER BY, of each set of rows with the same values.
Skips the first n rows of a result. The skipped rows are still read.
Paging by remembering the sort key of the last row shown and asking for the rows after it. Also called the seek method.
The last row's sort key, handed to the client as a token it sends back to get the next page.
`(a, b) < (x, y)`: compares the pairs left to right and stops at the first pair that differs.

explain_back.prompt: A nightly export copies a 50-million-row `ledger_entries` table, the app's list of every movement of money, 1,000 rows at a time with `ORDER BY entry_id LIMIT 1000 OFFSET :n`. It gets slower every hour, and sometimes it copies an entry twice. Explain both to a friend, and say what you'd change.
explain_back.answer: OFFSET doesn't jump. To skip n rows, PostgreSQL has to produce them, so batch number k reads about k times 1,000 index entries and throws away all but the last 1,000. The total work grows with the square of the number of batches, which is why each hour is slower than the last. The duplicates come from rows that change while the export runs. OFFSET counts positions, so an entry inserted with a lower entry_id after a batch was read pushes every later row one position down, and the next batch starts with the last row of the previous one. A deleted row does the opposite, and one row is skipped. The fix is keyset pagination: remember the last entry_id of each batch and ask for `WHERE entry_id > :last ORDER BY entry_id LIMIT 1000`. The index PostgreSQL keeps for the table's unique id lets each batch go straight to its start, so every batch costs the same, and no row is read twice. If the order were by created_at, the cursor would need entry_id as a tiebreaker in a row comparison, with an index on (created_at, entry_id).

deeper.body:
LATERAL doesn't always mean a loop. When the subquery has no LIMIT, no aggregate and no other reason to run per row, the planner (the part of PostgreSQL that picks how to run a query) can often turn it into an ordinary join. Then it may choose a hash join, which builds a lookup table from one side and probes it with the other, as it would for the same query written without LATERAL. The per-row plan appears when the subquery needs it, as LIMIT does. Read the plan: a Nested Loop with `loops` equal to the number of outer rows is the per-row form.

Going backward with a keyset cursor means flipping two things, the comparison and the sort. For the previous page, ask for `(created_at, payment_id) > (:first_created_at, :first_payment_id) ORDER BY created_at ASC, payment_id ASC LIMIT 20`, then reverse the 20 rows in your program. The same index serves both directions.

A total count, "page 3 of 51,231", is its own problem. `count(*)` over a million rows reads them all on every request, whatever kind of paging you use. Most screens do better with "more results" than with an exact total. When an estimate is enough, the planner's row estimate from EXPLAIN costs nothing, and so does `reltuples` in `pg_class`, PostgreSQL's own table about tables, for a whole table.

OFFSET has one more trap. A locking clause such as `FOR UPDATE` locks the rows a query reads, so nobody else can change them until you're done. With `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE ... OFFSET 100`, the rows that OFFSET skips are locked too, though they aren't returned. Lost updates: row locks, SKIP LOCKED and job queues, in the Transactions track, builds job queues with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and LIMIT, never OFFSET.

Finally, every list query in this lesson is fast only if an index matches its WHERE and ORDER BY in the right column order. Columns compared with `=` come first (card_id), then the sort key (created_at, payment_id). Indexes and reading EXPLAIN explains why that order matters, and how to read the plans that show it.
